objects.name: PSR J1745-2900
objects.note: A neutron star with a magnetic field of about 10^14 gauss, hundreds of trillions of times Earth's, found in 2013 when it flared in X-rays, then seen pulsing every 3.76 seconds in radio. The only pulsar known this close to Sgr A*, about a third of a light-year from it on the sky; its motion fits a star born in the clockwise disc.

young.about: The young massive stars of the central half parsec (Yelda et al. 2014's 116), each placed by its measured position on the sky and 3D velocity. Their distance along our line of sight isn't measured, so: from the disc's plane for the most likely members of the clockwise disc; from the measured acceleration towards Sgr A* where there is one (its size; the side from the disc, else drawn); else drawn. RA offsets and proper motions are east positive (checked: the members' velocities lie in the disc's plane and all turn clockwise only that way round).

cluster_stars.about: The nuclear star cluster's brightest red giants, as measured: where each is on the sky and how bright, from the GALACTICNUCLEUS survey; how far along our line of sight, drawn from the cluster's and the nuclear disc's shapes (so only those that land within the sphere are drawn).
notes: Galactic Centre stars (not foreground, from the Ks vs H-Ks diagram), detected in H and Ks, with the paper's Ks extinction for the star's own layer (layer 1 if detected in J, else layer 2); brighter than M_Ks -2.6 after the dust: the luminous giants, above the red clump (complete enough there despite the patchy dust and crowding: fainter, the survey's gaps round dark clouds and its pointings' seams would show as tunnels through the cluster)

The survey's central field covers every 0.5 pc cell within 9.8 pc of Sgr A* on the sky; each star is kept if its drawn depth puts it within 9 pc of Sgr A*, so the measured stars fill a sphere and the model's points the rest. They thin out from 5 pc (kept with chance 1 - smoothstep(5, 9, r): ours), so the sphere has no edge

Depth drawn from the line of sight's density, the cluster (flattened Dehnen) plus the nuclear disc (exponential), the galaxy model's own (galaxy_model.json nucleus), with Galactic north at its position angle at Sgr A*; seeded, so builds repeat

V from Ks: V - Ks from the median de-reddened H - Ks of the survey's Galactic Centre stars at the star's brightness (one star's is too uncertain: 5% in its extinction is ~0.1 mag in H - Ks), through Bessell & Brett's giant colours. The survey sets the red clump's (H - Ks)0 at 0.10, Bessell & Brett's K0-K1 III, so no shift between their systems. Tint: the close-up's red-giant colour (B - V 1.5) for all
refs: Nogueras-Lara, Schödel & Neumayer 2021, A&A 653, A133 (GALACTICNUCLEUS IV: its central field, 2,009,482 stars, with extinction and foreground flags; survey: Nogueras-Lara et al. 2019, A&A 631, A20), via scripts/tools/fetch_gns.py
Bessell & Brett 1988, PASP 100, 1134 (Table III, intrinsic colours of giants)

cnd.about: Its inner edge, lit by the young stars, glows as the minispiral's Western Arc.
cnd.drawn: Drawn as the dust in it, which hides what's behind: where its gas is from ALMA's map of HCN (a molecule found in dense gas), how far along our line of sight from the tilted disc its motions fit.
cnd.mass_note: Its mass is uncertain: estimates run from ~10,000 Suns (from its dust) to 100,000-1,000,000 (from its gas's lines; Requena-Torres et al. 2012, A&A 542, L21). Here HCN's brightness stands in for the gas's column (it saturates in the densest clumps), scaled to 50,000 Suns within 2 pc (Etxaluze et al. 2011). Even the lowest estimate makes the disc tens of magnitudes thick in visible light, so the choice matters only at its thin edges
cnd.select_note: Kept: emission above 4 sigma within 40 km/s of the disc's speed there (Ukani et al.'s measured spread: 5-40 km/s), 0.5-4 pc from Sgr A* in the disc's plane, faded out from 3.4 pc. Left out: gas at other speeds in the same part of the sky (streamers falling in, the clouds round the centre in front and behind: step 7)
refs: ALMA project 2017.1.00040.S (PI P.-Y. Hsieh; Hsieh et al. 2021, ApJ, doi:10.3847/1538-4357/abf4cd): HCN 1-0, the 12 m array's pipeline cube (beam 3.7 x 2.3 arcsec, 0.8 km/s), via scripts/tools/fetch_cnd_hcn.py

cmz.about: The Central Molecular Zone: the Galaxy's densest gas, tens of millions of Suns of it in giant clouds (the Brick, Sgr B2, Sgr C, the 20 and 50 km/s clouds) on streams round the centre, out to ~250 pc. Its dust hides what's behind it.
cmz.drawn: Drawn as its dust, which hides what's behind: how much along each sight line from Herschel's map of the dust's glow (the Galaxy's fore- and background taken out), each catalogued cloud at its measured distance along our line of sight, spread by its size; the gas round and between them at its nearest clouds' distances, shared among them by closeness on the sky, spread wider.
notes: 75% of the column lies outside the catalogued clouds: each such pixel's is shared among its 3 nearest clouds (weights exp(-d^2 / 2 (25 pc)^2), d on the sky), each part at that cloud's distance, spread by the cloud's size and 20 pc more (ours). Where streams on both sides overlap on the sky, it keeps both
A cloud's spread along our line of sight: its size on the sky (the radius of a circle of its pixels' area)

Within ~4.5 pc of Sgr A* on the sky the map's dust is the circumnuclear disc's (drawn from ALMA's HCN): taken out here, else it would go to a neighbouring cloud's distance, ~30 pc in front, and hide the nuclear star cluster
